nameStory: The violet wood-sorrel gets its name from its beautiful purple-pink flowers and its preferred woodland habitat. The 'sorrel' part comes from the sour taste of its leaves, which contain oxalic acid - the same compound that gives rhubarb its tangy bite.
description: Violet wood-sorrel is a charming low-growing perennial wildflower that forms small colonies in shaded areas. It typically reaches just 4-8 inches tall, with delicate three-part leaves that look like tiny shamrocks. The plant produces lovely five-petaled flowers that range from pale pink to deep violet, each about half an inch across. Unlike some of its yellow-flowered cousins, this species adds a splash of purple color to the forest floor.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five-petaled flowers in shades of pink to violet, about half an inch across, with darker purple veins running through the petals like delicate roadmaps

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three heart-shaped leaflets arranged like a shamrock, soft green and slightly fuzzy to the touch, with a distinctly sour taste when chewed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant that stays under 8 inches tall, spreading by underground bulbs to form small patches

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small pointed capsules that split open when ripe, explosively shooting tiny seeds several feet away when touched

habitat: Look for violet wood-sorrel in rich, moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly in areas with deep leaf litter. It thrives in partial to full shade under maple, oak, and beech trees, often growing alongside spring wildflowers like trout lily and wild ginger. You'll most commonly find it on gentle slopes and in woodland valleys with well-drained but consistently moist soil.

seasonality.spring: Flowers bloom from April through June, creating small purple carpets in the dappled sunlight of the forest floor before the tree canopy fully leafs out.
seasonality.summer: Leaves remain green and visible through summer, though flowering typically winds down by July in most areas.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to die back in late fall, with leaves turning yellow before disappearing completely.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible, surviving as small bulbs underground until spring returns.

funFact: When you touch the ripe seed pods of violet wood-sorrel, they explode like tiny cannons, shooting seeds up to 10 feet away - this dramatic seed dispersal method is called 'ballistic dispersal' and can actually startle you if you're not expecting it!
confusionNotes: With only 24 recorded observations in New England, violet wood-sorrel is much less common than the abundant yellow wood-sorrels found throughout the region. The purple flowers make it unmistakable when blooming - if you see purple flowers on a shamrock-leafed plant, you've found something special!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'wood-sorrel,' this plant is completely unrelated to true sorrels (which are in the buckwheat family). Both groups just happen to have sour-tasting leaves due to oxalic acid, leading to similar common names.
compareHints: Violet wood-sorrel is easily distinguished from its New England relatives by its purple flowers - all other common wood-sorrels in the region have yellow flowers. Mountain wood-sorrel has white flowers with pink veins, making violet wood-sorrel the only true purple-flowered member of the family you'll encounter here. The three-part shamrock leaves are identical across species, so flower color is your best identification clue.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mountain woodsorrel differs from its yellow-flowered relatives in the genus by having white petals with pink veins instead of bright yellow ones.
Among New England's woodsorrels, upright yellow woodsorrel stands tall while creeping woodsorrel sprawls flat along the ground.
Slender yellow woodsorrel is smaller and more delicate than upright yellow woodsorrel, with thinner stems that tend to sprawl rather than stand erect.
Creeping woodsorrel differs from its upright cousin (Oxalis stricta) mainly in its prostrate, mat-forming growth habit versus the upright's tall, erect stems.
Unlike other woodsorrels in New England which have green leaves and yellow flowers, false shamrock stands out with its deep maroon foliage and white or pink blooms.
Among New England's woodsorrels, this is the only one with large pink flowers - all the others have either small yellow blooms or purple ones.
Great yellow woodsorrel differs from its more common relatives like upright yellow woodsorrel and slender yellow woodsorrel by its significantly larger leaflets and more spreading growth habit.
Pink-sorrel stands out from New England's other woodsorrels primarily by its pink flowers - most relatives have yellow blooms, while violet woodsorrel has purple flowers.
